To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the medial temporal-lobe memory system plays a role in consolidation and that the process of consolidation can be modeled by a simple neural network.

(i) consolidation of memory is a process that takes place over time and that is dependent on the medial temporal lode system; (ii) the medial temporal lade system may serve to stabilize memories that have been formed in other brain regions; (iii) a neural network model can capture some key aspects of consolidation; (iv) this model is a modification of a standard Hopfield network in which synaptic connections are modified by a learning rule that depends on a Hebbian mechanism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: How does the brain store information?
the question: How does the brain store information in a way that is permanent and resistant to disruption?
the question of why the medial temporal lode is necessary for memory and how it contributes to the storage of memory traces.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the medial temporal lobes are involved in a process that allows memories to become consolidated and independent of the medial temporal lode.
the consolidation process involves the transfer of information from medial temporal lobe to neocortical structures.
consolidation is a process that takes time and that is mediated by the medial temporal lode memory system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
consolidation is a process that gradually transforms memories from a labile, hippocampus-dependent form to a more stable form that is independent of the hippocampus.
the model provides a simple and plausible account of how the hippocampus and adjacent cortex could be involved in consolidation.
the medial temporal lobes may serve as a temporary storage for memories that are being established in neocortical areas.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the process of consolidation can be explained by the interaction of two mechanisms: synaptic plasticity and the competitive interactions of memory representations.
the medial temporal system is a critical part of a larger memory system that involves other brain areas.

the medial temporal lobes play a role in memory consolidation, and that this role is consistent with the view that memories are initially encoded in a distributed fashion and gradually become more focused and stable over time.
